newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia set to pull out last troops from Chechnya.
newsitem.headline: Russia set to pull out last troops from Chechnya.

text.p: Russia's Defence Ministry will start pulling out its last troops from breakaway Chechnya on December 1 in line with pledges made by President Boris Yeltsin, Interfax news agency said on Wednesday.
The withdrawal will be completed by January 25, two days before presidential and parliamentary elections in the war-shattered region, it added.
Interior Ministry spokesman Vasily Panchenkov told Reuters his ministry would also withdraw its troops but gave no deadline, saying more would be known after November 30.
"When we talk about a withdrawal of federal troops it also includes Interior Ministry soldiers as they are all part of the same federal force," Pantshenkov added.

Russia has already withdrawn the bulk of its troops from Chechnya following an August 31 peace treaty that halted 21 months of conflict between Russian troops and separatists and deferred a final decision on the region's political status.
But Moscow had wanted to leave two units permanently in Chechnya -- one from the Defence Ministry and another from the Interior Ministry.
A surprise order last Saturday by Yeltsin that they should also be withdrawn outraged his communist and nationalist opponents in the State Duma lower house of parliament.
They plan to hold an extraordinary parliamentary session on Friday to discuss the issue, arguing that by withdrawing the troops Yeltsin is sanctioning Chechen independence.
They have threatened to try to impeach Yeltsin -- a long drawn-out procedure which has little chance of success -- or to call for a no-confidence vote in the government.

On Wednesday the RIA news agency said the Russian federal commander in Chechnya, Vladimir Sukhoruchenko, and the Chechen chief of staff had reached agreement "on all questions" relating to the practical withdrawal of Moscow's troops.
RIA quoted Sukhoruchenko as saying the Chechens had agreed to provide an escort to guarantee the security of his troops.

Interfax, citing an unnamed source in the general staff, said Russia's remaining troops in Chechnya numbered 6,000. The Defence Ministry also plans to remove 2,000 armoured vehicles, four tonnes of supplies and 400 tonnes of military equipment.
The Defence Ministry's brigade will be restationed in the southern Russian city of Budennovsk, where scores of people were killed in June 1995 when Chechen rebels took hostages at a local hospital.
Tens of thousands of people, mostly civilians, were killed in Chechnya after Yeltsin sent troops to crush the region's bid for independence in December 1994.
Elections to set up a post-war administration in Chechnya are scheduled for January 27 and the polling campaign officially began on Wednesday.

Chechen separatist leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev has already said he plans to run for the presidency and on Tuesday guerrilla leader Shamil Basayev, who led the Budennovsk raid last year, said he too would stand, Itar-Tass news agency said.
A third possible candidate is the respected Chechen Prime Minister Aslan Maskhadov, though he has so far shown loyalty to Yandarbiyev in order to avoid a split in separatist ranks.
Tass said Doku Zavgayev, the Kremlin-backed official who ran Chechnya during the war and who now lives in Moscow, would not return to the region to run in the election.
The Moscow News weekly called the upcoming elections "the start of peaceful construction of a state in Chechnya".

But it added that other regions of the former Soviet Union that had succeeded in wresting autonomy after a period of fierce fighting had mostly experienced a sharp fall in living standards and international isolation.
"It is now for Chechnya to prove that this rule has exceptions or to discover that its trials do not end with the conclusion of war," it added.
